abstract.p: Neurological disorders pose a challenge for targeted therapy due to restricted access of therapeutic agents to the central nervous system (CNS). Current methods are limited by procedure-related risks, invasiveness, and insufficient CNS biodistribution. A novel percutaneous transvenous technology, currently in clinical trials for communicating hydrocephalus, offers a minimally invasive approach by providing endovascular access to the cerebrospinal fluid-filled cerebellopontine angle (CPA) cistern. We hypothesized that drug delivery to the CPA cistern could yield widespread CNS distribution. Using an ovine model, we compared the biodistribution of scAAV9-CB-GFP following CPA cistern infusion with previously reported cisterna magna (CM) administration. Targeting both the CPA cistern and CM in sheep, we employed a lumbar spine-inserted microcatheter under fluoroscopy. CPA delivery of AAV9 demonstrated biodistribution and transduction in the cerebral cortices, striatum, thalamus, midbrain, cerebellum, and spinal cord, with minor liver distribution comparable to CM. The favorable safety profile in humans with hydrocephalus suggests that percutaneous endovascular injection into the CPA could offer a clinically safer and minimally invasive delivery system for CNS gene and cell-based therapies.

Benatti and colleagues describe a novel technique for accessing the cerebrospinal fluid-filled cerebellopontine angle (CPA) cistern adapted from a percutaneous transvenous technology, a minimally invasive treatment of communicating hydrocephalus in clinical trial phase, for the delivery of gene therapy to the CPA cistern in an ovine model.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Development of adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapies for the central nervous system (CNS) is challenging due to the presence of the blood-brain barrier (BBB).1 Methods to overcome this challenge include development of AAV serotypes with enhanced CNS tropism2 or alternative delivery methods. Current methods to access the CNS include intrathecal, cisterna magna, or intracranial injection,3 but these methods are either insufficient to achieve widespread distribution or highly invasive. The gene therapy field needs alternative safe CNS delivery techniques to enhance the effectiveness of AAV therapies.4

Currently, CNS targeting relies on various routes: intravenous (i.v.), intraparenchymal (i.p.), and intra-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), with the latter including intracerebroventricular (i.c.v.), cisterna magna (CM), or intrathecal (i.t.). Regardless of the therapeutic agent of choice, each delivery strategy to the CNS exhibits distinct advantages and disadvantages. I.v. delivery depends on capsids capable of crossing the BBB and lack of AAV seropositivity of patients.5,6 Additionally, the i.v. route requires high doses of AAV, which can significantly increase costs and the potential for off-target adverse effects.7,8 Direct brain targeting can be achieved by i.p. delivery (i.e., convection-enhanced delivery), which requires an invasive surgical approach.3 However, this approach carries risks of injury associated with the invasiveness of the procedure and potential deleterious effects due to a high MOI at the site due to the infusion volume required.3,9,10 CNS targeting via CSF largely overcomes the challenges of the BBB, the presence of neutralizing antibodies, and the risk of parenchymal brain injections.11,12 I.c.v. injection allows administration of larger volumes (compared to i.p.) with widespread expression in periventricular areas and the superficial cerebral cortex; however, i.c.v. injection results in reduced distribution in deep brain structures.13,14,15 Additionally, this method requires a burr hole through the skull and a catheter passed through brain parenchyma. Although i.c.v. access is routine for the treatment of hydrocephalus, associated risks include brain injury and intracerebral hemorrhage.16 Lumbar i.t. puncture is convenient and easy, but robust transduction is limited to the hindbrain and spinal cord.17 CM injection may achieve superior biodistribution in the brain,18,19 but drawbacks include risks of medullar injury and drug escape along the needle tract due to surface tension.20 More recently, we developed a safe technique to catheterize the CM through the lumbar i.t. space to deliver AAV; however, we also observed low transduction of deep brain structures.21

A novel, percutaneous, endovascular technique to safely access the CSF-filled cerebellopontine angle (CPA) cistern located at the base of the brain, anterior to the pons/brain stem, has been developed (eShunt System, CereVasc, Boston, MA, USA). This catheter access system is presently in the clinic to deliver a transdural CSF shunt implant into the CPA cistern for the treatment of communicating hydrocephalus (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05232838, NCT05501002, NCT04758611, and NCT05250505).22 In this approach, a catheter is navigated from a transfemoral venous approach into the internal jugular vein and then into the inferior petrosal sinus, an intracranial dural venous sinus that travels along the skull base, where it crosses the dura lining the vein wall to access the adjacent CSF-containing CPA cistern. The entire system is deployed through percutaneous access to the femoral vein, with no need for open surgery. The eShunt implant is seated into the vessel wall and anchored into the CPA, where it passively drains CSF into the jugular vein, and is being explored in clinical trials for the treatment of communicating hydrocephalus (Figure 1).22,23 The eShunt delivery catheter provides direct access to the CSF-filled CPA cistern, enabling injection of AAV and other gene- and cell-based therapies.Figure 1
Transvascular access and location of the CPA cistern
(A) I.v. anatomical map of access to the CPA. Access begins with catheterization of the deep femoral vein and ascends cranially through the venous vascular system, represented by the yellow dashed line, reaching the internal jugular vein and subsequently the inferior petrosal sinus. The yellow star represents the puncture site to access the CPA. (B) Illustration of the transvascular approach to treating hydrocephalus that is in the clinic for the treatment of communicating hydrocephalus. In both images, the red circle indicates the location of the CPA cistern. Adapted from Lylyk et al.22 (C) Three-dimensional reconstruction of the anatomical location of the human CPA. The pons and CM are highlighted for anatomical reference. This figure was created using BioRender (BioRender.com).

Considering the risk and limitations of current CNS delivery techniques and the potential utility of this technology as a catheter drug delivery system, here we evaluated CPA cistern injection as a delivery route for AAV gene therapy. Since the cerebral vasculature is within the confined space of the CPA, we hypothesized that improved biodistribution may be achieved to brain areas that receive arterial supply from these arteries, especially those fed by the anterior inferior cerebral artery and basilar artery.

sec.title: Results
sec.p:
Sheep and non-human primates have similar CPA anatomy compared to humans (Figure 2A). Since non-human primates are highly prone to stroke during neuro-endovascular procedures (M.J.G. and H.L.G.-E., unpublished data), sheep were selected for the present study. Ungulates, which include sheep and pigs, have an anatomical difference called a rete mirabile that prevents navigation to cerebral vasculature from peripheral veins.24 Therefore, to evaluate CPA infusion as a delivery route, we used a modification of our previously published i.t. navigation method into the CM to guide an endovascular microcatheter into the CPA (n = 4), which was confirmed by computed tomography (CT) and MRI neuroimaging (Figures 2B and 2C). These data were compared to sheep receiving CM injections (n = 4) using the same delivery approach as described previously.21Figure 2
Comparison of anatomical location of the CPA cistern between species and intraoperative images
(A) All images show a ventral view of the brain stem of different species. The species name is indicated above the respective image. For anatomical reference, black arrows indicate the optic chiasm. The yellow asterisk represents the location of the CPA cistern. (B) MRI/CT overlay from the sheep procedures. The white arrow highlights catheter tip placement in the CPA cistern of the sheep. (C) Contrast enhancement at the CPA during injection in sheep. The black arrow highlights catheter tip placement in the CPA cistern of the sheep.

sec.title: CPA cistern delivery of AAV9 transduces cells throughout the brain and spinal cord of sheep 3 weeks following infusion
sec.p:
CPA delivery of the scAAV9-CB-GFP vector resulted in broad transduction of cells in the CNS. GFP immunohistochemistry showed extensive transduction in frontal, parietal, and temporal cerebral cortices that subjectively appeared more prominent in the CPA cohort as compared to the CM cohort (Figure 3A). We observed cortical transduction of neurons and astrocytes but not oligodendrocytes or microglia. Interestingly, transduction in the hippocampus was primarily neuronal, along with select regions of the deeper brain regions, including the thalamus, caudate, and putamen (Figure 3A). In the cerebellum, Purkinje cells were widely transduced, with GFP positivity evident in both the cell bodies and processes (Figure 3A). Deep cerebellar nuclei were also transduced in both cohorts, but scant positivity was observed in the molecular and granule cell layers (data not shown). In the spinal cord, there was also transduction of lower motor and sensory neurons throughout the entire length of the spinal cord, shown here in sections of the cervical and lumbar spine (Figure 3A). No non-specific binding of GFP antibody in untreated sheep tissue was observed.Figure 3
Transduction and biodistribution of scAAV9-CB-GFP after CPA cistern and CM delivery
(A) Sections from cortical regions showing GFP-positive neurons and glial cells. Subcortical structures with less exposure to CSF show fewer GFP-positive neurons and glia. While discrete GFP expression was detected in the striatum in the cortex of animals receiving injections into the CPA cistern, there was no GFP expression in the striatum of animals injected with AAV in the CM. (B) Graphical representation of the quantitative lateralized distribution of vector genomes (vg) in selected areas of the brain of animals injected with scAAV9-CB-GFP in the CPA cistern, demonstrating the difference between the injected (ipsilateral) and non-injected (contralateral) side. (C) Graphical representation of the quantitative distribution of vg in selected areas of the CNS and liver of animals injected with scAAV9-CB-GFP in the CPA cistern versus animals injected with the same vector in the CM. ∗p < 0.05.

sec.title: Biodistribution of AAV9 vector genomes in the brain and spinal cord of sheep 3 weeks following CPA cistern infusion delivery
sec.p:
qPCR was performed to assess vector genome (vg) biodistribution of scAAV9-CB-GFP throughout the CNS and liver. The areas of the CNS assayed were the frontal cortex, parietal cortex, temporal cortex, occipital cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain, and cervical and lumbar intumescence. The highest genome copies were detected in the midbrain, which is the closest area to the injection, followed by the occipital cortex, striatum, thalamus, lumbar intumescence, parietal cortex, cervical intumescence, frontal cortex, and temporal cortex (Table 1). We also assessed for laterality in biodistribution after CPA injection, and no notable hemispheric differences were observed in biodistribution after CPA injection. sec.title: Comparison of biodistribution and cell transduction between CPA cistern delivery and CM delivery
sec.p:
Vg quantification of the frontal cortex, temporal cortex, striatum, thalamus, and midbrain demonstrated equivalent biodistribution of scAAV9-CB-GFP in CPA-injected animals (data shown above) compared to the CM cohort. The occipital cortex was the only region that had statistical significance with approximately 4-fold greater biodistribution in CM cohort animals compared to the CPA cohort (p = 0.019). A 2.6-fold increase trend toward increase was observed in the parietal cortex of the CPA cohort compared to the CM cohort (p = 0.15). In the spinal cord, the CPA-injected animals showed similar transduction in the lumbar intumescence compared to CM-injected animals; this was reflected in the vg data (cervical intumescence [CI] p = 0.29, lumbar intumescence [LI] p = 0.24). Only modest biodistribution to liver tissue was observed with both injection routes, an order of magnitude lower than that observed in CNS tissues (Figure 3C; Table 2). sec.title: Immunofluorescence co-localization of anti-GFP and specific neural cell markers shows astrocyte and neuronal GFP transduction following CPA infusion delivery
sec.p: The CPA delivery of the scAAV9-CB-GFP vector resulted in broad transduction of cells throughout the CNS. Immunofluorescence staining for GFP, combined with co-localization analysis using the specific neural cell markers NeuN (neuronal nuclei), GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein), Iba1 (ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1), and Olig2 (oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2), revealed GFP expression exclusively in neurons and astrocytes.

As shown in Figure 4, the co-localization of GFP with NeuN and GFAP demonstrated pronounced GFP expression in astrocytes and neurons. Importantly, areas with high levels of GFP expression did not show GFP co-localization with Olig2, indicating that oligodendrocytes did not express GFP. Furthermore, while microglia did not translate GFP themselves, some microglia displayed well-defined areas of GFP, suggesting phagocytosis of GFP-expressing cellular debris.Figure 4
Co-Localization of GFP with Specific Neural Cell Markers Following CPA Delivery of scAAV9-CB-GFP Vector
Representative immunofluorescence images showing co-localization of GFP with neural cell markers in the CNS. GFP (green) co-localizes with NeuN (neuronal marker, red) and GFAP (astrocyte marker, red), indicating transduction in neurons and astrocytes, respectively. White arrows indicate cells where GFP is co-localized with the specific cell marker. Notably, GFP expression is robust in astrocytes and in neurons. Some microglia display well-defined areas of GFP, indicated by white arrows, indicating phagocytosis despite the cell itself not translating the protein. No co-localization of GFP Olig2 (oligodendrocyte marker) is observed, suggesting the absence of GFP expression in oligodendrocytes. The scale bar represents 100 μm.

These findings highlight the selective transduction efficiency of the scAAV9-CB-GFP vector in astrocytes and, to a lesser extent, in neurons following CPA delivery. The absence of GFP in oligodendrocytes and the observed phagocytosis by microglia in areas of high transduction further underscore the specificity of the vector for astrocytes and neurons within the targeted regions of the CNS.

sec.title: Dorsal root ganglia and liver histopathology analysis
sec.p: The dorsal root ganglia (DRGs) analyzed from the experimental cohorts were compared to a non-injected control and analyzed for DRG toxicity as described by Bennet et al.25 (Figure S1). No evidence of DRG toxicity was observed, nor were there any other noteworthy differences in the DRGs between the experimental and control groups. Similarly, necropsy revealed no macroscopic findings in the liver that would suggest toxicity. Representative sections of liver lobes were analyzed and compared to non-injected controls and literature,26 with no noteworthy differences identified (Figure S2).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Recent clinical27 and preclinical19,21,28 studies have demonstrated the efficacy and safety of AAV infusion into the CM. Despite its rare and obsolete use in clinical practice outside of the gene therapy field, and lack of a trained physician workforce for its performance, the CM route has gained recent interest from investigators looking to deliver AAVs to the brain. Nevertheless, the CM technique exhibits inherent risks, since the puncture is performed at the base of the skull, close to the brain stem. These risks may include injury to the medulla or nearby vertebral arteries. The CM exhibits substantial anatomic variability, with as many as 25% of patients demonstrating a CM that is absent, small and slit like, or with cerebellar tonsils in contact with the occipital dura, which may complicate access.29 Additionally, due to surface tension and the exposure of the access site to the atmosphere, there is a potential risk of therapeutic leakage along the needle tract, extending through the subcutaneous and muscle tissues. Further, the low level of current clinical use of the CM puncture technique necessitates significant procedural development and operator training to expand the approach beyond a select few, highly specialized institutions. Often, the risk associated with puncture of the CM presents the dilemma of choosing between alternative, safer injection sites with lower therapeutic potential or assuming the risks of CM. Considering recent first-in-man evidence demonstrating the ability to safely access the CPA transvenously using an endovascular catheter system,22 we delivered scAAV9-CB-GFP to the CPA cistern, resulting in broad biodistribution and cell translation throughout the CNS. This technique provides minimally invasive access to CSF at the base of the brain for single-dose administration using the existing clinical device, with the possibility of implanting a subcutaneous reservoir for repeat access to the CPA cistern for multi-dose therapies such as antisense oligonucleotides. Compared to delivery via the CM, direct administration into the CPA achieved broad distribution of the vector in the cerebral cortex, cerebellum, and spinal cord. This approach could be useful in treating neurological disorders that could benefit from gene delivery throughout the CNS by bypassing the BBB via a less invasive approach compared to conventional routes of administration. Importantly, it could leverage the same large established workforce and neuroangiography imaging, procedural pathways, and clinical care teams currently in place for the endovascular treatment of large-vessel occlusion stroke.30

The increased susceptibility of non-human primates (NHPs) to stroke in association with neuro-endovascular procedures remains poorly understood (M.J.G. and H.L.G.-E., unpublished data). Instances of stroke occurrence in NHPs, potentially influenced by factors such as catheter size, highlight the need for caution when employing this species for neuro-interventional studies. However, it is important to note that, in clinical neuro-interventional practice, endovascular catheters are routinely utilized and are regarded as safe and lifesaving. Therefore, while stroke risks in NHPs warrant careful consideration in research settings, they are not likely to pose significant concerns in clinical practice. To address these considerations, we opted for sheep as our experimental model, following the precedent set by Taghian et al.21 Sheep have a large brain and blood flow dynamics comparable to humans, providing a practical model for studying neuro-interventional delivery techniques.31,32 Additionally, sheep have been employed extensively in various research fields, including gene therapy,13,21,33,34 offering valuable insights into the translational potential of our findings while also enhancing the relevance of our findings to clinical applications.

Vector quantification demonstrated broad distribution in the cortices, midbrain, and cerebellum. Similar to reports of CM injection, transduction of deep brain structures (i.e., striatum and thalamus) was modest. Limited exposure of deep structures to CSF likely explains the reduced transduction of deep brain structures. Additionally, the exposure time of CSF35 and cellular affinities during diffusion toward deeper structures also likely impacts the level of cell transduction. To overcome this limitation, direct parenchymal injection may be necessary for the effective treatment of neurodegenerative diseases that mainly affect the striatum or thalamus, since this type of intervention results in superior transduction of deep brain structures.13,36,37

In this study, a self-complementary AAV was chosen over a single strand. Unlike single-stranded vectors, which require a second-strand synthesis step prior to RNA and protein expression, self-complementary vectors bypass this process, resulting in faster and more robust expression. This attribute was particularly advantageous for our study, as we aimed to achieve high and rapid expression levels of the transgene in sheep. Overall, we observed a greater number of transduced astrocytes and neurons in the forebrain, which is a feature of the AAV payload used in this study. The modified chicken β-actin promoter (CB) used in this AAV vector construct includes a truncated intron to enable packaging into a self-complementary vector. This alters the expression pattern associated with the traditional chicken β-actin (CBA) promoter, with the modified CB promoter exhibiting predisposed expression in protoplasmic astrocytes in the gray matter.21 In a previous study, the scAAV2/PHP.B-GFP vector was examined in 6-week-old C57BL/6 mice following i.v. injections. Notably, this investigation revealed an exceptional degree of astrocyte transduction within the cortex, facilitated by a ubiquitous CBA promoter. However, similar to our findings, the observed neuronal transduction was notably lower than previously documented levels.38 Use of a neuronal specific promoter would likely increase the number of GFP-positive neurons, and payload should be taken in to account to tailor to the desired distribution of the transgene.21 Building upon these findings, ongoing studies are currently exploring the effects of alternative promoters within self-complementary AAV vectors, aiming to elucidate their impact on transduction efficiency and specificity. It is becoming increasingly evident that the level of transgene expression varies considerably between cell types, encompassing both the number of cells expressing the transgene and the strength of expression. Moreover, this variability is influenced by the specific regulatory elements employed,39 highlighting the complexity of gene expression regulation in AAV-mediated gene therapy approaches.

Data from the present study demonstrate transduction of scAAV9-CB-GFP into lower motor neurons throughout the entire length of the spinal cord, demonstrating that CPA administration has at least efficiency comparable with other delivery approaches targeting the spine. The distribution of AAV throughout the spinal cord after i.t. delivery is well established for several species.11,18,21 CM delivery represents a viable and reliable alternative for uniform biodistribution of viral vectors throughout the entire spinal cord of NHPs,21,40 while the effectiveness of lumbar i.t. AAV delivery on transducing the entire spinal cord remains controversial. While Hinderer et al. demonstrated that only the vector administered into the CM of NHPs will distribute evenly throughout the spinal cord,40 different studies showed a relatively even level of transduction to the entire spinal cord after CM or lumbar i.t. injection.11

As reported in previous studies, delivery of AAV directly into the CSF does not restrict its biodistribution to the CNS.41,42 In the present study, we detected modest levels of scAAV9-CB-GFP vector in the liver, with values equivalent to that published previously (∼1 × 104 vg/100 ng of DNA),21 after delivery of the same vector construct in sheep after CM injection using a microcatheter. Sparse GFP expression has been observed in the liver of NHPs that received AAV9 via CM infusion, suggesting reduced peripheral vector exposure with this delivery modality.15 Preferential transduction of liver by AAV that escapes the CNS has been well documented.42

The absence of notable findings can probably be attributed to the animals being euthanized at just 3 weeks post injection. This time frame is considered short for the degeneration of the DRGs to become apparent, as indicated by earlier research. Studies suggest that a longer observation period might be necessary to observe significant DRG degeneration.43 Similarly, the lack of observed liver toxicity aligns with recent reviews suggesting that hepatic involvement after systemic AAV infusion manifested between 8 and 20 weeks post treatment, with patients experiencing lethal subacute immunotoxic reactions within this time frame.44

This transdural catheterization into the CPA cistern presents distinct advantages over CM delivery. Notably, degenerative changes in the human spine, leading to spinal stenosis, pose a contraindication for CM delivery, making CPA an attractive alternative for gene therapy in patients with bone/joint involvement or degenerative disc disease. CPA delivery mitigates risks such as myelitis, infection, and complications from CSF leakage. Its versatility extends to transvascular delivery, offering promise for multi-dose AAV, repeated administrations of oligonucleotide-based therapeutics, cell-based therapies, CRISPR-based therapies, and small molecules within the CNS. In the context of repeated administrations, crucial for achieving long-term therapeutic effects, we draw inspiration from the success of nusinersen in spinal muscular atrophy,45 highlighting the eShunt system’s role in facilitating repeat access. This capability is vital for sustained therapeutic outcomes in CNS-targeted therapies, exemplified by prolonged exposure to nusinersen in CNS tissue. Moreover, the CPA cistern approach, easily performed by neurointerventional operators, overcomes the limitations of CM injection, marked by invasiveness and a scarcity of physicians trained for the procedure.

Here, we provide proof-of-concept data for delivery of AAV into the CPA in a large animal. Our results suggest that administration of gene therapy into the CPA cistern achieves broad and diffuse distribution throughout the CNS and is at least equivalent to CM administration. In light of the favorable safety profile observed with clinical use of CPA transdural catheterization to treat communicating hydrocephalus,22,46 percutaneous endovascular injection into the CPA cistern may provide a clinically safer, minimally invasive method for delivery to the CNS that provides an improved balance of invasiveness and efficiency4 compared to existing routes of administration.

sec.title: AAV vector
sec.p: scAAV9-CB-GFP, in an AAV serotype 9 capsid, carries an expression cassette that contains a modified version of the CB promoter with a truncated SV40 intron (CB promoter; Figure S3), GFP cDNA, and a bovine growth hormone (BGH) poly-adenylation (poly(A)) signal.21 The vector was produced by triple transfection and purified by cesium chloride gradient, as described previously.47 The formulation was then dialyzed in Dulbeccos’s PBS without calcium and magnesium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).21,48

sec.title: Animal use and study approval
sec.p: All experimental studies involving animals were approved by the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School Institutional Animal Care and Use committee. Sheep (mixed males and females) weighing between 23 and 27 kg were used for this study. Cohorts include animals receiving injections into the CPA cistern (n = 4) or CM (n = 4). Sheep were pre-medicated with a combination of buprenorphine SR (0.27 mg/kg), given 24 h before the procedure day, and acepromazine (0.05 mg/kg) and glycopyrrolate (0.004 mg/kg), both given on the procedure day. Flunixin meglumine (1.1 mg/kg) was administered as an anti-inflammatory. Sheep were anesthetized using ketamine (10 mg/kg) and midazolam (0.2 mg/kg) and intubated. Anesthesia was maintained by isoflurane gas (1%–3%). After AAV administration, animals were kept in house for 21 days, receiving water and hay ad libitum.

sec.title: Pre-surgical MRI
sec.p: MRI was performed on a 3-T whole-body MRI scanner (Ingenia, Philips Healthcare, Best, the Netherlands) using an 8-channel knee coil. Multi-slice T1- and T2-weighted turbo spin-echo and 3D magnetization-prepared rapid gradient-echo were acquired with a field of view of 128 × 128 × 80 mm3, an in-plane resolution of 1 × 1 mm, and a slice thickness of 2 mm. Total imaging time was approximately 25 min.

sec.title: I.t. catheter placement and guide to the CPA cistern or CM
sec.p: The animals were positioned in the prone position for the procedure and vector infusion. The lumbosacral region was shaved and aseptically prepared following standard procedures. A cone-beam CT was acquired and registered with the previously acquired MRI as described previously.21 The lumbar puncture was performed by using a 17G × 3.5-in Tuohy spinal needle at the lumbosacral intervertebral space (L7–S1). A 1.7-French outer diameter intravascular microcatheter (SL-10, Stryker Neurovascular, Fremont, CA, USA) was introduced into the subarachnoid space via the Tuohy needle. Under fluoroscopic guidance overlayed on the fused CT/MRI used as a roadmap, the microcatheter was navigated over a 0.014-in Synchro micro guide wire (Stryker Neurovascular) into the CPA cistern (n = 4) or into the CM (n = 4). Although rare, when necessary, an “S” wire shape tip advanced slightly distal to the catheter. The microcatheter was guided ventral to the spinal cord.

For CPA injection, when close to the craniocervical junction, the microcatheter was directed laterally, with the tip of the microwire distal to the microcatheter, or the microwire was torqued while inside the microcatheter because of the “S” shape that was given to the tip was enough to rotate the microcatheter toward the desired location in the proximity of the temporal bone at the level or slightly superior to the inner ear. Cone-beam CT (Allura Xper FD20 system) was repeated to confirm adequate catheter position relative to bony and neural structures. After confirming the catheter position, 1 mL of iodinated contrast material (Omnipaque 240 mg/mL, GE Healthcare) was slowly injected to identify the distribution pattern of the contrast material prior to vector injection. Once the location of the catheter tip was confirmed by imaging, 2.7 mL of scAAV-CB-GFP vector was infused at 100 μL/min. Animals were sacrificed 3 weeks post injection.

sec.title: ScAAV-CB-GFP injection
sec.p: For the experimental procedures in this study, we adapted the methodology described by Taghian et al.21 with modifications to suit our experimental requirements. In the referenced study, Taghian et al. utilized a total injection volume of 15 mL, administered at a rate of 1 mL/min, with a viral vector titer of 1.2 E13 vg/mL, resulting in a total vector dose of 1.8E14 vg. Importantly, this study focused on the i.t. injection of the viral vector into the CM, which provides a relatively larger CSF pocket.

In contrast, our study targeted the CPA cistern, characterized by a smaller CSF pocket compared to the CM. To achieve a comparable vector dose while accommodating the anatomical differences, we adjusted the injection parameters accordingly. Specifically, we administered a reduced injection volume of 2.7 mL, delivered at a rate of 100 μL/min. Despite the reduction in volume, we maintained a viral vector titer of 6.67E13 vg/mL to ensure an equivalent total vector dose to that employed by Taghian et al..

By adapting the injection parameters to suit the specific anatomical location and experimental requirements of our study, we aimed to ensure the effective delivery of the viral vector while maintaining consistency with the overall vector dose utilized in the reference study.

sec.title: Tissue harvesting and preparation
sec.p: Animals were euthanized with pentobarbital (180 mg/kg i.v.) and the brain, spinal cord, and liver were collected. The brains were transversely sectioned into 4-mm blocks, extending from the frontal lobe to the most caudal aspect of the cerebellum/brain stem. Each slice was alternately frozen in a dry ice-isopentane bath and stored at −80°C or fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin. Part of representative segments of the spinal cord at the rostral cervical, mid-cervical, CI, thoracic, thoracolumbar, mid-lumbar, and LI levels were collected frozen in a dry ice-isopentane bath and stored at −80°C or fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin.

sec.title: Qualitative assessment: Immunostaining and image acquisition
sec.p: Selected formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) blocks were cut at 5-μm thickness. Staining was performed using Leica Autostainer XL (Leica Biosystems, IL, USA) with anti-GFP primary antibody (Abcam, ab290, 1:1,000) in Signal Stain (Cell Signaling Technology, 8112L) and amplifier antibody goat anti-rabbit immunoglobulin G (IgG) (Vector, MP-7601) and ImmPRESS horseradish peroxidase horse anti-goat IgG (Vector, MP-7601). Slides were counterstained with Gill II hematoxylin.

sec.title: Qualitative assessment: Immunofluorescence co-localizing GFP with specific neural cell markers
sec.p: FFPE blocks were cut as described in the previous section. The slides were stained with following primary antibodies: chicken anti-GFP (1:1,000, ab13970, Abcam, Cambridge, UK), rabbit anti-NeuN (1:200, ab177487, Abcam, Cambridge, UK), rabbit anti-GFAP (ready-to-use solution, GA524, Dako, Agilent Technologies, Glostrup, Denmark), rabbit anti-Iba1 (1:200, CP290A, BioCare Medical, Pacheco, CA, USA), and rabbit anti-Olig2 antibody (1:200, ab109186, Abcam, Waltham, MA). Alexa-conjugated secondary antibodies (donkey anti-rabbit 555 and goat anti-chicken 488) were used. Images were obtained using Leica Thunder Imager DMi8 (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany).

sec.title: Quantitative assessment: Biodistribution analyses via qPCR
sec.p: Vg copy numbers from different regions of the CNS (frontal cortex, temporal cortex, parietal cortex, occipital cortex, thalamus, striatum, midbrain, cerebellum, brainstem, CI, and LI) and peripheral tissues (liver and nerves) were determined by qPCR. DNA extraction was performed using the DNeasy blood and tissue kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany). QPCR was targeted to the BGH poly(A) using the forward primer 5′-CCTCGACTGTGCCTTCTAG-3′, reverse primer 5′-TGCGATGCAATTTCCTCAT-3′, and probe 56-AM/TGCCAGCCA/ZEN/TCTGTTGTTTGCC/3IABkFQ. The lower limit of detection in the qPCR assay was 100 vg/100 ng of DNA, and any sample below this limit was considered non-detectable. Experimental results are shown as mean ± SD. An unpaired heteroscedastic Student’s t test was performed using GraphPad Prism v.9.3.1 (GraphPad, San Diego, CA, USA) to evaluate for statistical difference.

To determine the average number of GFP vg per cell, we employed qPCR analysis, as described above. Following qPCR analysis, the results were expressed as vg per 100 ng of DNA. To normalize these data to a per-cell basis, we divided the vg count by 100, yielding the vg per 1 ng of DNA. Finally, to ascertain the average vg per cell within each sampled CNS structure, we further divided this value by 152—we utilized the established conversion factor of 1 ng of DNA corresponding to 152 diploid genomes, representing a single cell.49 This sequential process allowed us to quantify the average number of GFP vg present per cell in the analyzed CNS structures.

sec.title: DRG and liver analysis
sec.p: FFPE blocks were cut as described in the previous section and sectioned at 5-μm thickness. H&E staining was performed. For histopathological analysis, sections containing DRGs or liver were specifically selected and examined under a Leica Thunder Imager DMi8. The morphology and overall cellular architecture were assessed to evaluate any potential pathological changes.
